title: Document TEI-first self-hosting strategy and architecture
description:
Document the preferred self-hosting architecture for Code Scout using TEI (Text Embeddings Inference) as the recommended solution for all platforms.

**Research Findings:**

## TEI is the Preferred Self-Hosting Solution

**Why TEI for All Platforms:**
1. **Mac (Apple Silicon)** - Metal acceleration, still fastest option despite no CUDA
2. **Linux/Windows with NVIDIA GPU** - Blazingly fast with CUDA acceleration
3. **Purpose-built for embeddings** - Outperforms vLLM for embedding workloads
4. **Cross-platform** - Single solution works everywhere

## Ollama Trade-offs

**Still viable but with caveats:**
- Simple setup, auto model switching
- **Performance issue:** No real concurrency for batching
- Model switching overhead significant with batches
- Best for: Small repos, development, simplicity over speed

## TEI Wrapper Solution

**Emulate Ollama's hot-swap feature:**
- Thin wrapper around TEI detects model switch needs
- Auto-loads document model when code pass completes
- **Bonus:** Pre-loads code model in background after docs pass
- Enables use of full nomic-embed-code (7B) model
- Better performance than Ollama with same UX

## Background Embedding Daemon

**Improved AI Agent UX:**
- Run embedding in background loop (file watcher)
- AI agents only use search, never trigger indexing
- Auto-reindex on file changes (debounced)
- Keep manual CLI trigger for git hooks, manual control
- Daemon manages TEI wrapper lifecycle

**Cloud Hosting:**
- Still an option via OpenAI-compatible providers
- Most don't host nomic-ai models (paid alternatives)

**Documentation Tasks:**
- Update TEI_SETUP.md for cross-platform (CUDA + Metal)
- Document TEI wrapper architecture and rationale
- Document background daemon design
- Update README with TEI-first recommendation
- Explain performance: TEI > Ollama, why not vLLM

title: Implement TEI wrapper with model hot-swapping and pre-loading
description:
Build a lightweight HTTP wrapper around TEI that provides Ollama-like model hot-swapping while enabling use of the full nomic-embed-code (7B) model with better performance.

**Why This Wrapper:**

**Problem with running two TEI instances:**
- nomic-embed-code (7B) uses ~4-8GB RAM per instance
- Running both code + text models = ~8-16GB RAM total
- Too heavy for many development machines

**Problem with Ollama:**
- No real concurrency for batching
- Model switching overhead kills performance with --workers >2

**Solution: Smart TEI Wrapper:**
- Single TEI process, one model loaded at a time
- Wrapper detects model switch requests
- Stops TEI, restarts with new model
- Pre-loads next model in background after pass completes
- Better performance than Ollama, lower memory than dual TEI

**Requirements:**

1. **OpenAI API Compatibility**
   - Expose POST /v1/embeddings endpoint
   - Accept OpenAI request format: {"model": "...", "input": [...]}
   - Return OpenAI response format
   - Support Authorization header (pass-through or optional)

2. **Model Management**
   - Track currently loaded model
   - Detect when requested model differs from loaded
   - Stop current TEI process gracefully
   - Start new TEI process with requested model
   - Cache model load state
   - Handle concurrent requests during model switching (queue or reject)

3. **Background Pre-loading**
   - After code pass completes, detect pattern
   - Pre-load text model in background
   - After text pass completes, detect pattern
   - Pre-load code model in background
   - Configurable pre-load behavior (on/off, which model)

4. **TEI Integration**
   - Manage TEI process lifecycle (start/stop/restart)
   - Forward embedding requests to TEI
   - Handle TEI startup time (~2-3 seconds)
   - Graceful error handling (TEI crashes, OOM, etc.)

5. **Configuration**
   - TEI binary path (default: text-embeddings-router)
   - TEI port (default: 8080, internal)
   - Wrapper listen port (default: 11434, Ollama-compatible)
   - Model mappings (alias support)
   - Pre-load settings

6. **Performance**
   - Queue requests during model switching
   - Return 503 with Retry-After header during switch
   - Minimal overhead when model already loaded
   - Connection pooling to TEI

**Tech Stack:**
- Language: Go (matches code-scout codebase)
- Framework: net/http or gin-gonic/gin
- Location: cmd/tei-wrapper/

**Models Supported:**
- nomic-ai/nomic-embed-code (7B, 26GB) - code embeddings
- nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (137M, 262MB) - text embeddings
- nomic-ai/CodeRankEmbed (137M, 521MB) - alternative code embeddings

**Success Criteria:**
- code-scout index works with wrapper exactly like Ollama
- Wrapper auto-switches between models as needed
- Pre-loading reduces subsequent pass startup time to near-zero
- Memory usage: single model at a time (~4-8GB max)
- Performance: Better than Ollama (higher concurrency)
- Clear error messages and status reporting

**Implementation Notes:**
- Use os/exec to manage TEI process
- Signal handling for graceful shutdown
- Health check endpoint for monitoring
- Logging for debugging model switches

title: Implement background embedding daemon with file watcher
description:
Create a background daemon that automatically re-indexes the codebase on file changes, eliminating the need for AI agents to trigger indexing manually.

**Why Background Daemon:**

**Current UX:**
- AI agents must remember to run 'code-scout index' after changes
- Interrupts workflow, adds cognitive overhead
- Easy to forget, leading to stale search results
- Manual CLI trigger required

**Improved UX with Daemon:**
- AI agents only use 'code-scout search'
- Indexing happens automatically in background
- Always-fresh search results
- Manual trigger still available for git hooks, manual control

**Requirements:**

1. **File Watching**
   - Monitor repository for file changes (create, modify, delete)
   - Respect .code-scout-ignore patterns
   - Watch code file extensions (.go, .py, .js, .ts, .java, .rs, etc.)
   - Watch documentation files (.md, .txt, .rst)
   - Debounce: Wait for file activity to settle before indexing

2. **Debouncing Strategy**
   - Wait N seconds after last file change (default: 5s)
   - If more changes during wait, reset timer
   - Prevents re-indexing during active editing
   - Configurable debounce interval

3. **Incremental Indexing**
   - Only re-index changed files when possible
   - Full re-index on major changes (schema, config)
   - Track file modification times
   - Content-based deduplication (already implemented)

4. **Daemon Lifecycle**
   - Start: 'code-scout daemon start'
   - Stop: 'code-scout daemon stop'
   - Status: 'code-scout daemon status'
   - Logs: 'code-scout daemon logs'
   - Auto-start on first search if not running?

5. **Process Management**
   - Background process (fork/daemon)
   - PID file in .code-scout/daemon.pid
   - Graceful shutdown (SIGTERM)
   - Crash recovery (auto-restart?)
   - Manages TEI wrapper lifecycle if used

6. **Configuration**
   - Daemon enabled/disabled flag
   - Debounce interval (default: 5s)
   - File patterns to watch
   - Indexing concurrency (--workers, --batch-size)
   - Log level and output

7. **Status Reporting**
   - Current status (idle, watching, indexing)
   - Last index time
   - Files watched count
   - Pending changes count
   - TEI wrapper status

8. **Integration with TEI Wrapper**
   - If TEI wrapper is running, use it
   - If not, start it automatically
   - Manage wrapper lifecycle
   - Handle wrapper failures gracefully

**Tech Stack:**
- Language: Go
- File watcher library: fsnotify or similar
- Location: cmd/code-scout/daemon.go (new subcommand)

**Commands:**


**Success Criteria:**
- Daemon detects file changes within 1 second
- Re-indexing starts 5 seconds after last change
- Only changed files are re-indexed (incremental)
- AI agents can search without ever running index
- Manual 'code-scout index' still works (bypasses daemon)
- Daemon survives TEI wrapper crashes/restarts
- Clear status reporting for debugging

**Implementation Notes:**
- Use fsnotify for cross-platform file watching
- Store daemon PID in .code-scout/daemon.pid
- Logs to .code-scout/daemon.log
- Signal handling for graceful shutdown (SIGTERM, SIGINT)
- Consider systemd integration for Linux
- Consider launchd integration for macOS

**Future Enhancements:**
- Git-aware: Only index on commit/branch switch
- Remote daemon: Watch remote repos over SSH
- Multi-repo support: One daemon, many repos
- Web UI for status monitoring
- Metrics: Files indexed, search latency, etc.

title: Fix Linux cross-compilation build failure from macOS
description:
The build.sh script fails when cross-compiling for Linux from macOS due to CGO dependencies.

**Problem:**
When running ./build.sh on macOS, the darwin builds succeed but linux_amd64 fails with:
```
# runtime/cgo
linux_syscall.c:67:13: error: call to undeclared function 'setresgid'
linux_syscall.c:73:13: error: call to undeclared function 'setresuid'
```

**Root Cause:**
Cross-compiling Go code with CGO from macOS to Linux requires a Linux C toolchain. The macOS C compiler cannot compile Linux-specific system calls (setresgid, setresuid) because it's using macOS SDK headers.

**Current Workaround:**
Only build darwin targets locally (works fine).

**Potential Fixes:**

**Option 1: Skip Linux builds on macOS** (simplest)
- Detect host platform in build.sh
- Only build matching platform + architectures
- Document that Linux builds require Linux host or CI/CD

**Option 2: Use Docker** (recommended for local Linux builds)
- Add Dockerfile with Go + LanceDB dependencies
- Mount source code into container
- Build Linux binaries inside container
- Works on any host platform

**Option 3: Install cross-compiler toolchain**
- Install Linux cross-compilation toolchain on macOS
- Configure CGO to use cross-compiler
- More complex setup, harder to maintain

**Option 4: CI/CD only** (recommended for production)
- Use GitHub Actions or similar for Linux builds
- Keep local builds simple (host platform only)
- Distribute via releases

Recommend: Option 2 for local development, Option 4 for releases.

title: Bug: Ignored files not removed from metadata.json despite cleanup message
description:
**Bug Description:**
When running `code-scout index`, files that are now ignored by .gitignore or .code-scout-ignore show a message saying they are being removed, but they remain in `.code-scout/metadata.json` after the indexing completes.

**Current Behavior:**
1. User adds patterns to .code-scout-ignore (e.g., `examples/`, `test_data/`)
2. Runs `code-scout index`
3. Output shows: "Removing N changed/deleted file(s) from index..."
4. Files remain in metadata.json with their old modification times

**Expected Behavior:**
Ignored files should be completely removed from metadata.json during the cleanup phase at lines 220-223 in index.go.

**Root Cause:**
The deletion logic at index.go:220-223 deletes from `metadata.FileModTimes` map, but the metadata may not be getting saved correctly, or there's an issue with the SaveMetadata implementation.

**Location:**
cmd/code-scout/index.go:220-223

**Test Case:**
1. Index a repo with examples/ and test_data/
2. Add those patterns to .code-scout-ignore
3. Run index again
4. Check .code-scout/metadata.json - files should be gone but they persist

**Priority:** P1 - This breaks the ignore feature's promise of excluding files from the index.
close_reason: Fixed metadata persistence bug. Metadata deletion and save now happen immediately after chunk deletion, and before early return when no files need indexing. This ensures ignored files are removed from metadata.json.

title: Parameterize build.sh to support selective target building
description:
Modify build.sh to allow developers to choose which platform targets to build.

**Current behavior:**
- build.sh hardcodes targets based on available lib/ directories
- Always attempts all targets (darwin_amd64, darwin_arm64, linux_amd64)
- Fails on incompatible cross-compilation (macOS → Linux with CGO)

**Desired behavior:**
Option 1: Environment variable (simple)
```bash
# Build only darwin targets
TARGETS="darwin_arm64 darwin_amd64" ./build.sh

# Build only linux
TARGETS="linux_amd64" ./build.sh

# Build everything (current behavior)
./build.sh
```

Option 2: Platform detection (smart defaults)
```bash
# On macOS: only build darwin_* by default
# On Linux: only build linux_* by default
./build.sh

# Override to build all
TARGETS="all" ./build.sh
```

**Implementation:**
- Parse TARGETS environment variable
- Filter available lib/ directories based on selection
- Default to host-compatible targets only (detect via uname)
- Clear messaging about which targets are being built/skipped

**Success criteria:**
- Developers can specify which targets to build
- Default behavior doesn't fail on cross-compilation
- Clear output showing which targets were built/skipped
